name: Compilers & Runtimes
description: Lexing, parsing, IR, optimisation, JIT vs AOT and what actually happens between your source and the CPU.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Compilers & Runtimes is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a compiler?
cards.answer: A program that translates source code written in one language into another, usually lower-level, form — native machine code (C, Rust, Go) or bytecode for a virtual machine (Java, C#) — before the program runs.
cards.explanation: Compiling ahead of time lets the compiler check the whole program for errors and optimise it, so the result runs fast. The trade is an extra build step between editing code and running it.

resources.title: Crafting Interpreters — A map of the territory

cards.prompt: Compiler vs interpreter
cards.answer: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs; an interpreter executes the program directly, statement by statement. Many real systems mix both.

left.title: Compiler
points: Output runs fast on its own

right.title: Interpreter
points: Errors found when the line runs
Shell scripts, classic Python and Ruby

cards.explanation: The line is blurry in practice: CPython compiles to bytecode and then interprets it, and JavaScript engines interpret first and JIT-compile hot code. "Compiled language" really describes the usual implementation, not the language itself.

cards.prompt: Define source code, assembly, machine code and bytecode.
cards.answer: Source code is what programmers write. Machine code is the binary instructions a specific CPU executes. Assembly is a human-readable text form of machine code (`mov`, `add`, `jmp`). Bytecode is a compact instruction set for a virtual machine (the JVM, .NET, CPython) rather than for real hardware.
cards.explanation: Machine code is tied to a CPU architecture (x86-64, ARM64), which is why native programs are built separately per platform. Bytecode is portable: the same `.class` file runs on any JVM.

cards.prompt: What is just-in-time (JIT) compilation?
cards.answer: Compiling code to native machine code while the program is running, typically only for the "hot" parts executed most often. It combines an interpreter's quick start-up with near-compiled speed.
cards.explanation: JIT compilers can optimise using information only available at run time, such as which types actually flow through a function. They power the JVM, .NET and every major JavaScript engine.

cards.prompt: What is a runtime (runtime environment)?
cards.answer: The supporting software a program needs while it runs: memory management (allocation and garbage collection), threads, error handling, the standard library and often a JIT. Examples: the JVM, the .NET CLR, Node.js, the Go runtime.
cards.explanation: Even "runtime-free" languages have a small one — C has its C runtime start-up code that calls `main`. The bigger the runtime, the more it does for you, and the more it costs in start-up time and memory.

cards.prompt: What is a transpiler?
cards.answer: A source-to-source compiler: it translates code into another language at a similar level of abstraction — TypeScript to JavaScript, modern JavaScript to older JavaScript (Babel), or Sass to CSS.
cards.explanation: Transpilers let you write in a nicer or newer language while still running on platforms that only understand the target. Browsers only run JavaScript and WebAssembly, so the web depends heavily on them.

modules.name: The Compilation Pipeline
modules.description: From characters to machine code, stage by stage.

cards.prompt: What are the stages of a typical compiler?
cards.answer: Lexing (characters → tokens), parsing (tokens → AST), semantic analysis (types, scopes, symbol tables), IR generation, optimisation passes, then code generation and register allocation.
cards.explanation: The front end is language-specific, the back end is target-specific, and a shared IR in the middle is what lets LLVM serve dozens of languages and architectures. Errors are reported at the earliest stage that can detect them — which is why type errors come after syntax errors.

resources.title: Crafting Interpreters — A map of the territory

cards.prompt: What is an AST, and how does it differ from a parse tree?
cards.answer: An abstract syntax tree keeps the meaningful structure of the program and discards syntactic noise — parentheses, semicolons, precedence scaffolding. A concrete parse tree contains every grammar production.
cards.explanation: ASTs are what linters, formatters, transpilers, codemods and IDE refactorings operate on. Tools such as `ast-grep` or Babel let you pattern-match structure instead of text, which is why they can rewrite code that regex cannot safely touch.

cards.prompt: JIT vs AOT compilation
cards.answer: AOT compiles before execution with no runtime knowledge; JIT compiles at runtime and can specialise on observed behaviour.
cards.explanation: The JVM and V8 tier up: interpret, then lightly optimise, then aggressively optimise hot code with guards that bail out if assumptions fail. That is why microbenchmarks must warm up, and why AOT (GraalVM native image, .NET AOT) wins for short-lived serverless processes.

cards.prompt: Static vs dynamic typing
cards.answer: Static typing checks types before execution; dynamic typing checks them at runtime when an operation is performed.

left.title: Static
points: Whole classes of errors caught at compile time
Type system can obstruct valid programs

right.title: Dynamic
points: Fast to write, flexible at runtime
Needs more tests to reach the same confidence

cards.explanation: Orthogonal to strong vs weak typing, which is about implicit coercion: Python is dynamic but strong (`'1' + 1` errors), JavaScript is dynamic and weak (`'1' + 1` is `'11'`). Gradual typing (TypeScript, mypy) tries to buy the static benefits incrementally.

cards.prompt: Why might the optimiser delete this null check entirely?
cards.answer: Dereferencing `p` is undefined behaviour if it is null, so the compiler may assume `p` is non-null from that line on — making the check provably false and removable.
cards.explanation: Optimisers reason from the assumption that UB never happens. This is the root of many 'the compiler broke my code' reports and of real kernel CVEs where a null check vanished. Check before you dereference, and build with sanitisers.

resources.title: LLVM Blog — What every C programmer should know about undefined behavior

cards.prompt: What does a linker do, and what is the difference between static and dynamic linking?
cards.answer: It resolves symbol references across object files and libraries and lays out the final image. Static linking copies the library into the binary; dynamic linking records a dependency resolved at load time.
cards.explanation: Static gives a self-contained binary and no version skew, at the cost of size and no shared security patching. Dynamic gives smaller binaries and system-wide updates, at the cost of dependency hell — which is exactly what containers were invented to contain.

cards.prompt: CPython compiles source to ___ , which the virtual machine then interprets.
cards.answer: bytecode
cards.explanation: The `.pyc` files in `__pycache__` are cached bytecode, not machine code. Java does the same with class files on the JVM. The distinction 'compiled vs interpreted' is about implementation, not language — there are C interpreters and Python compilers.

modules.name: Lexing, Parsing & Types
modules.description: Tokens and grammars, parsing strategies, precedence, scopes and type inference.

cards.prompt: What does a lexer produce, and why is it a separate stage from parsing?
cards.answer: A stream of tokens — each with a kind (identifier, number, `+`, keyword), its text and its source position — while discarding whitespace and comments. Tokens are defined by regular expressions, which a simple, fast state machine can match.
cards.explanation: Separating the stages keeps the parser working on a small alphabet of meaningful symbols. Source positions attached to tokens are what make good error messages possible ("line 12, column 8") — lose them and every later stage reports errors vaguely.

cards.prompt: Why can a regular expression tokenize a language but not parse it?
cards.answer: Regular languages cannot count or nest — they cannot match arbitrarily deep parentheses. Programming languages have nested structure, which needs a context-free grammar and a parser with a stack (recursive descent, LL or LR).
cards.explanation: This is the Chomsky hierarchy in practice: regular (finite automata) ⊂ context-free (pushdown automata) ⊂ context-sensitive. It is exactly why "parse HTML with regex" fails, and why a lexer plus a parser is the standard split.

cards.prompt: What is a recursive-descent parser, and how does it handle operator precedence?
cards.answer: A hand-written parser with one function per grammar rule, each calling the others — `expression()` calls `term()`, which calls `factor()`. Precedence comes from the layering: lower-precedence rules call higher-precedence ones, so `*` binds tighter than `+`.
cards.explanation: Most production compilers (GCC, Clang, Go, TypeScript, Rust) use hand-written recursive descent because it gives the best error messages and recovery. Pratt parsing (precedence climbing) handles many operator levels compactly. Parser generators (yacc, ANTLR) suit DSLs.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `*` binds tighter than `+`; `**` is right-associative, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9`; unary minus on a base needs parentheses in JavaScript (`-2 ** 3` is a SyntaxError); and comparison operators bind looser than arithmetic. Encoding precedence and associativity is a core job of the parser.

cards.prompt: What does semantic analysis do after parsing?
cards.answer: It builds symbol tables and resolves every name to its declaration (respecting scopes and shadowing), checks types, and enforces rules the grammar cannot express — definite assignment, return types, access modifiers, and that `break` appears inside a loop.
cards.explanation: Lexical (static) scoping means a name resolves by where code is written, not where it runs — which is what makes closures work and lets the compiler resolve variables to fixed slots ahead of time instead of by name at runtime.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between local type inference and Hindley–Milner inference?
cards.answer: Local inference fills in types from nearby information — `var x = new List<int>()`, `let x = 5`, `auto` — flowing mostly forward from initialisers. Hindley–Milner (ML, Haskell, largely Rust within a function) infers types for whole functions by generating constraints and unifying them, often needing no annotations at all.
cards.explanation: Full inference is powerful but can produce confusing errors far from the real mistake, which is why languages that support it still encourage annotations on public signatures. TypeScript uses bidirectional local inference plus contextual typing.

modules.name: IR, Optimisation & Runtimes
modules.description: SSA, classic optimisations, register allocation, calling conventions, bytecode VMs and WebAssembly.

cards.prompt: What is SSA form, and why do optimisers use it?
cards.answer: Static single assignment: every variable is assigned exactly once, so each version gets a new name (`x1`, `x2`), and φ (phi) functions merge values where control-flow paths join. Each use then points to exactly one definition.
cards.explanation: That one-definition property makes data-flow analyses — constant propagation, dead-code elimination, value numbering — simple and fast. LLVM IR, GCC's GIMPLE, V8's TurboFan and the Go compiler all use SSA-based IRs.

cards.prompt: Name the classic compiler optimisations and what each does.
cards.answer: Constant folding and propagation (compute known values at compile time), dead-code elimination, common subexpression elimination, inlining (replace a call with the body), loop-invariant code motion, strength reduction (`x * 2` → `x << 1`), and vectorisation (use SIMD instructions for loops).
cards.explanation: Inlining is the enabling optimisation: it exposes the callee to every other optimisation in the caller's context. It is also why virtual calls, function pointers and cross-module calls (without LTO) are slower — the optimiser cannot see through them.

cards.prompt: What is register allocation, and what happens when it runs out of registers?
cards.answer: Mapping an unlimited set of IR values onto the CPU's small set of registers (16 general-purpose on x86-64). Values live at the same time interfere and need different registers; when there are not enough, some are spilled to the stack and reloaded when needed.
cards.explanation: Classic approaches colour an interference graph (NP-hard in general, so heuristics are used) or use linear scan, which is faster and common in JITs. Spills cost memory traffic, which is one reason tight loops with too many live variables slow down.

cards.prompt: What is a calling convention, and what is an ABI?
cards.answer: A calling convention fixes how functions pass arguments (which registers, what stack order), return values, and which registers the caller versus callee must preserve. An ABI is the wider binary contract: calling conventions plus data layout, name mangling, exception handling and system calls.
cards.explanation: Code compiled by different compilers or languages interoperates only if it shares the ABI — which is why FFI goes through the C ABI (`extern "C"`), why C++ ABI breaks force rebuilds, and why Windows x64 and System V (Linux/macOS) pass arguments differently.

cards.prompt: Tree-walking interpreter vs bytecode virtual machine
cards.answer: A tree-walker evaluates the AST directly by recursing over nodes; a bytecode VM first compiles to a compact linear instruction stream, then runs it in a tight dispatch loop.

left.title: Tree-walking
points: Fine for config languages and prototypes

cards.explanation: Bytecode is much faster (better cache locality, no pointer chasing, cheap dispatch) and is the design behind CPython, the JVM, Lua and Ruby's YARV. Stack-based VMs (JVM, CPython) have simpler compilers; register-based VMs (Lua, Dalvik) execute fewer instructions.

cards.prompt: What is WebAssembly, and what is it good for?
cards.answer: A portable, sandboxed binary instruction format that browsers and standalone runtimes compile to native code. C, C++, Rust, Go and others compile to it, running at near-native speed alongside JavaScript.
cards.explanation: It suits CPU-heavy work in the browser (codecs, image processing, games, CAD) and, via WASI, portable sandboxed plugins and edge functions on the server. It does not replace JavaScript for DOM work — calls across the boundary have a cost, and it has no direct DOM access.

cards.prompt: What is a transpiler, and what problem do source maps solve?
cards.answer: A source-to-source compiler: TypeScript to JavaScript, modern JavaScript to older JavaScript (Babel), Sass to CSS. A source map is a JSON file mapping positions in generated code back to the original source, so debuggers and stack traces show the code you wrote.
cards.explanation: Publishing source maps to production exposes your original source; many teams upload them privately to their error tracker instead. Without them, a minified stack trace pointing at "line 1, column 48210" is nearly useless.

cards.prompt: Writing a language's compiler in the language itself — compiled first by an earlier compiler — is called ___.
cards.answer: bootstrapping (self-hosting)
cards.explanation: Go, Rust, C#, TypeScript and GCC are self-hosting. It proves the language is capable and lets its authors use it daily, but raises the "trusting trust" question Ken Thompson posed: a compromised compiler binary can reinsert a backdoor into every future compiler built with it. Reproducible and diverse double-compilation builds defend against that.
